boreaz midifile fixtures

Every `.mid` beside this file is generated by `tools/midifile_fixtures.py` and none of them is
meant to be edited by hand. A binary file nobody can read is a fixture that quietly stops meaning
anything, so the recipe is the authority and the bytes are the build product: a reviewer reads the
builder, and a wrong fixture is one command away from correct again.

    python tools/midifile_fixtures.py --verify "boreaz midifile fixtures"   # what is committed is what the recipe says
    python tools/midifile_fixtures.py "boreaz midifile fixtures"            # rewrite this directory
    python tools/midifile_fixtures.py --out somewhere/else "boreaz midifile fixtures"

That header argument is the first line of this file and it is required. It asks whoever regenerates
the fixtures to have read this directory at all, which is the cheapest way to stop a fixture being
refreshed by accident: a generated asset nobody chose is a generated asset nobody reviewed.

The bytes are fully determined by the script - no clock, no random, no dictionary ordering - so two
runs produce identical files. That is what lets `tests/golden/midifile.txt` hold five measurements
per file instead of a shrug, and `--verify` is worth running in CI for exactly that reason.

| file | what it is for |
|---|---|
| `lead-simple.mid` | eight ascending eighths, one tempo, one track: nothing may be dropped, and one of each thing we accept that is not a note (a volume wheel, a pitch bend that leaves and returns) |
| `pad-chords.mid` | format 1, a chord across four tracks, a tempo change in a fifth track nobody plays, and the four parts we drop named out loud |
| `bass-running-status.mid` | running status from the second event to the last, and note offs spelled as note on with velocity zero |
| `glissando-88.mid` | all 88 keys A0 to C8 in order with the tempo halved halfway up, so a key mapped to the wrong pitch cannot hide |

The rude files are not here. A header cut short, a track shorter than its own declared length, a
chunk with an unknown name, a tempo of zero microseconds: those are built byte by byte in
`tests/test_midifile.cpp`, next to the message each one is expected to produce. A generated file
cannot be "the first six bytes of itself" without someone first saying what "itself" is, and a
fixture whose bytes live further from the assertion than the assertion does is a fixture that fails
for reasons nobody can read.

Two things here are load bearing beyond the obvious:

- The order of events that share a tick is the order in the file, deliberately, and the tests say so
  in words. A render that reordered a chord would produce a different waveform from the same notes,
  which makes a golden file a coin toss and a stereo image a rumour.
- Velocities and note counts are chosen so the arithmetic is checkable by hand: 88 keys, 24 chord
  notes against a 16 voice pool, a crescendo from 40 to 120. A fixture whose numbers only a program
  can explain is an assertion nobody checks.
